name: Dughall Mor and the Reelig Glen giants

location.address: Reelig Glen, near Kirkhill, Highland (Forestry and Land Scotland; car park off the A862)

story:
Britain's tallest tree lost its title to a neighbour standing about 55 yards away. Both are Douglas firs in Reelig Glen, a wooded glen west of Inverness. The older champion is Dughall Mor, Gaelic for Big Douglas, a name it got from a local competition. It was measured at 62 metres in 2000 and reported at 64 in 2005, and for a while no tree in Britain was known to be taller. Then the Reelig Glen Fir beside it was measured at 66.4 metres in 2014, by laser and by climbing, and reported as the new tallest tree in the UK. Wikipedia's list of superlative trees now gives 66.3 for it and 63.8 for Dughall Mor, which it ranks second. Heights this great shift with method and year, so read it as a close race.

The glen was planted from the 1800s by the Fraser family, much of it credited to James Baillie Fraser, a traveller in the Himalaya. The Forestry Commission bought it in 1949. Every tree in the stand is over a century old and many are around 50 metres. One list says Dughall Mor was planted in 1882, a date we could not confirm.

The honest catch is telling them apart. A bark label on Dughall Mor was reported missing in 2022, and a walker that summer could not be sure she had found it. Our pin is approximate. The Tall Trees Walk, about a mile, is free.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise the stand as the tallest firs in the glen, close together beside the Moniack Burn path south of the car park, near the information board. Dughall Mor and the Reelig Glen Fir stand about 55 yards apart.
access: Free to walk; Forestry and Land Scotland woodland with a waymarked Tall Trees Walk (about 1 mile) from the Reelig Glen car park. Parking charges apply at some FLS sites, check before going.
transport: No useful public transport; about 7 miles west of Inverness by the A862/A833 road, drive to the Reelig Glen car park.
recognise_facts: Tallest firs in the glen stand close together beside the Moniack Burn path, south of the car park, near the information board; an old bark label on Dughall Mor was reported missing in 2022.
The neighbouring Reelig Glen Fir stands about 55 yards from Dughall Mor.
verify_notes: Collectible point: the glen's cluster of giant Douglas firs, folding two named trees about 55 yards apart. DUGHALL MOR (Gaelic 'Big Douglas', named after a local competition): measured 62 m in 2000 (scottish-places.info), 64 m in 2005 (gillianswalks, quoting earlier reports), 63.8 m on Wikipedia's superlative list, which says planted 1882 (unsourced here, treat as claim). Once Britain's tallest tree. Neighbour 'Reelig Glen Fir': 66.3 m on Wikipedia's list (laser plus climb; Inverness Courier/Scotsman reports said 66.4 m in 2014), took the UK tallest title from Dughall Mor. A 2009 climbing forum thread disputes rankings (Argyll tree 63.79 m); not a source. Wikipedia list says Dughall Mor ranks second. Glen planted from the 1800s by the Fraser family; James Baillie Fraser (1783-1856, Himalayan traveller) credited with much of it. Forestry Commission bought the glen in 1949. All trees over 100 years old, many about 50 m. The Scotsman article was 403 (not read). Heights from fetched pages: scottish-places.info (62 m, 2000), Wikipedia list (63.8 and 66.3 m), gillianswalks (64 m in 2005, 66.4 m in 2014). PIN: only a Geograph geotag (57.45038,-4.4015, 2008, photo of the tree's Famous Tree sign) lands near the stand; photographer's point not proven on the individual trunk, so approximate, and a walk-through wood is not a small site. ALIVE: walker's blog dated 7 July 2022 describes the walk and the stand; she could not be sure she found Dughall Mor. No reports of storm loss found (searched Arwen/Eunice/Isha/Jocelyn context); lifecheck gives OLD (2008 only). Flagged: thin recent confirmation of which individual trunk. Dunkeld lead notes warn a blog mislabels Reelig as Hermitage: not repeated here, Hermitage Douglas fir is a different, fallen tree (2017).

name: Lord President's Oak

location.address: Culloden Wood, beside the Lord President's Seat stone and the bridge over the Highland railway, on the path to St Mary's Well, Inverness

story:
This oak was planted, by the account of the people who manage the wood, because a railway needed a stone moved. The stone was a seat used by Duncan Forbes of Culloden, Lord President of the Court of Session, and his wife. Forbes died in 1747. In 1855 the seat had to be moved for the Highland railway, and an oak was planted beside it around then. Hence the name, and an age of roughly 170 years.

The planting story comes from a single nomination, so treat it as the wood's tradition rather than a record. In 2020 Forestry and Land Scotland put the tree forward for Scotland's Tree of the Year and called it one of the most impressive in the country. The articles never say which oak it is, sessile or pedunculate, and nobody has published its girth. If you know your oaks, the acorn stalks will tell you, and we would like to hear.

It stands at the boulder still called the Lord President's Seat, just south of the bridge over the railway, on the trail to St Mary's Well. In 2024 a walker described the boulder below an old tree, without calling it an oak, which is the most recent sighting we have. The same walk passes the Prisoners' Stone and St Mary's clootie well.

It is a 19th-century tree, not a veteran, and the walk is free from the Culloden Wood car park, about five miles east of Inverness.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old oak over the Lord President's Seat, a boulder just south of the railway bridge on the Culloden Wood trail. The stone was moved here in 1855 for the Highland railway.
access: Free; Forestry and Land Scotland woodland, on the waymarked Culloden Wood Trail to St Mary's Well, on foot from the Culloden Wood car park.
transport: Culloden Wood is about 5 miles east of Inverness; bus services run to Culloden village (check current timetable), then walk into the wood; otherwise drive.

location_site.name: Lord President's Seat stone, Culloden Wood

recognise_facts: Stands at the Lord President's Seat, a boulder just south of the railway bridge on the wood trail.
The oak is named for the stone seat beneath it, which was moved here in 1855 for the Highland railway.
verify_notes: Nominated for Scotland's Tree of the Year 2020 by Laura McNally of Forestry and Land Scotland, hailed one of the most impressive in Scotland (Ross-shire Journal, 27 Aug 2020, fetched). Planted around 1855, said to be after the stone seat used by Duncan Forbes, Lord Culloden (1685-1747, Lord President of the Court of Session) and his wife had to be moved for the Highland railway (Ross-shire Journal 2020; Highland HER MHG30100 gives the stone moved in 1855 for the railway and the Moray Firth view story from the FLS car park board). The planting date is therefore a claim from a news nomination, not a documented record; age is derived and broad, 'roughly 170 years'. Species is not named in the articles I fetched, only 'oak': ask the reader. Girth and height not published in anything fetched. Pin: Highland HER grid reference NH 7216 4557 for the stone converted to WGS84 (57.48229, -4.13389), 4 m by 4 m; the tree stands at the stone, so a small named site, but the oak itself is not mapped: approximate. ALIVE: Inverness Courier walk piece of 1 April 2024 describes a boulder 'below an old tree' just south of the railway (does not name the tree as an oak); no storm loss found. FLS visit page 404 and the P&J article 403. Flagged: single-source planting story, species unnamed. A candidate for a reader-confirmed species and girth. Not a veteran: it is a 19th-century planting, worth the walk for the story (Culloden estate, Forbes, Tree of the Year nominee) and for the Culloden Wood walk, which also passes the Prisoners' Stone and St Mary's clootie well.
